Let
\[
f:\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb R\setminus\{1\}
\]
be surjective and satisfy the two given identities.

Putting \(x=1\) in the first equation gives
\[
0=f(1)(f(-y)-1).
\]
Since \(f(-y)\ne1\), we obtain \(f(1)=0\). Putting \(y=1\) then yields
\[
f(x)=f(x)f(-1)-f(x),
\]
so, since \(f\) is not identically zero, \(f(-1)=2\).

Now put \(x=-1\) in the first equation. Using \(f(-1)=2\), we get
\[
f(-y)=2f(y)-2+f(y)=3f(y)-2.
\]
This calculation is incorrect because the first equation gives instead
\[
f(-y)=f(-1)f(-y)-f(-1)+f(y)=2f(-y)-2+f(y),
\]
hence
\[
f(-y)=2-f(y).
\]
Define \(g(x)=f(x)-1\) and \(h(x)=-g(x)=1-f(x)\). Then \(h\) is odd and
\[
h(xy)=h(x)h(y),\qquad h(1)=1.
\]
Moreover, because \(f\) is surjective onto \(\mathbb R\setminus\{1\}\), \(h\) is surjective onto \(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\), and therefore \(h(x)\ne0\).

For \(x\ne0,1\), write \(t=h(x)\). Since \(f(x)=1-t\), the second condition gives
\[
1-h(1-t)=\frac{t}{t-1},
\]
so
\[
h(1-t)=\frac1{1-t}.
\]
As every \(t\ne0,1\) occurs, this implies
\[
h(u)=\frac1u\qquad(u\ne0,1).
\]
Also \(h(1)=1=1/1\). Thus \(h(u)=1/u\) for every \(u\ne0\), and consequently
\[
\boxed{f(x)=1-\frac1x}.
\]

This function has image \(\mathbb R\setminus\{1\}\), satisfies the first identity by direct expansion, and satisfies the second because
\[
f(f(x))=-\frac1{x-1}=\frac1{1-x}=\frac1{f(1/x)}.
\]
Hence it is the unique solution.
